title: Many prints, one stamp to fix
allegory: Broadcasting is one rubber stamp pressed onto every page; when each page comes back with a red-pen correction, the stamp's fix is all the corrections added together, because nudging the stamp changes every print at once.
map: the original small tensor, e.g. a bias b of shape (3,)
broadcasting b up to the batch shape (4, 3)
the upstream gradient for each broadcast copy
adding every correction onto the one stamp
summing the gradient over the broadcast dims
the gradient must match the original shape: prepended dims summed away, stretched size-1 dims summed but kept
credit: The 'a value used more than once must add up (+=) its gradients' point follows Andrej Karpathy's micrograd video, The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation.

cap.1: You add one small row of numbers to every row of a batch. Going backwards, its gradient comes back batch-sized, too big to fit the thing it belongs to.
cap.2: x + b with x of shape (4, 3) and b of shape (3,) broadcasts b to (4, 3). Backward hands you a (4, 3) gradient, but b.grad must be (3,).
cap.3: The upstream gradient has the broadcast output's shape. Your autograd must map it back to each input's own shape, or the parameter update fails or silently misaligns.

cap.1: One stamp pressed onto four pages. Each page comes back with a red-pen correction. To fix the stamp, you add up all four corrections.
cap.2: Broadcasting reuses one value in many places. Each place sends back its own gradient, and the value's total gradient is the sum of all of them.
cap.3: Multivariable chain rule: if b feeds outputs y₁..yₙ then ∂L/∂b = Σᵢ ∂L/∂yᵢ · ∂yᵢ/∂b. For a broadcast copy each ∂yᵢ/∂b is 1, so it is a plain sum.

cap.1: The stamp's fix is every page's correction added together. Nudge the stamp and every print moves at once, so every print gets a say.
cap.2: In code, for a bias broadcast over the batch: b.grad = grad_out.sum(dim=0). A value used n times gets n gradient terms, and they add.
cap.3: Broadcasting is a linear copy map; the backward pass of a linear map applies its transpose, and the transpose of copying is summing. Expand forward means sum backward.

cap.1: Four pages of corrections, one column per letter on the stamp. Add each column down and the stamp gets 4, 5 and 6. Four rows fold into one.
cap.2: grad_out is (4, 3); summing over dim 0 gives the (3,) gradient for b. The batch dimension only existed because of the broadcast.
cap.3: unbroadcast: first sum away the leading dims that were prepended; then sum with keepdim=True over every dim where the original had size 1. The result has the input's exact shape.

chapters.name: Add, never average
chapters.verdict: A value used n times gets n gradients, added. Averaging is a silent bug.

cap.1: Averaging the corrections sounds fair, but it is wrong. The stamp really did cause every print's mistake, so every correction counts in full.
cap.2: Using mean instead of sum still gives the right shape, so nothing complains. The parameter just learns n times too slowly.
cap.3: mean divides the true gradient by the broadcast extent; shapes agree, so only a numerical gradient check catches it. Compare against finite differences when you write backward functions.

chapters.name: Where it hides
items: A bias shared by every example
One conv kernel at every position

cap.1: The same rule holds wherever one thing is used many times: a bias added to every example, one stencil slid over a whole image, one word vector reused.
cap.2: Bias grads sum over the batch; a conv kernel's grad sums over every position; an embedding row's grad sums over every time its token appears.
cap.3: Weight sharing always means gradient accumulation. When you later read gradients to understand a model, a shared weight's gradient is a sum over every use, not any single one.

coda.title: Tap to raise one page's correction, then see where it lands

readouts.label: stamp shaped (4, 1): sum over dim 1, keepdim

caption.1: Tap cells to raise one page's correction. Watch where it lands for each stamp shape: a row stamp, a column stamp, a single dot.
caption.2: Tap one cell: it adds exactly one to one entry of each summed gradient. The mean row moves only a quarter as far, which is the bug in miniature.
caption.3: Each original element's gradient is the sum over the cells it was copied into. The broadcast decides the sum: (3,) sums rows, (4, 1) sums columns with keepdim, () sums all.

micrograd's classic bug: a value used twice must += its gradient

hamming.what: The backward half of broadcasting: summing a gradient back down to the shape of the tensor that was stretched.
hamming.when: Whenever you write the backward pass of an op whose inputs were broadcast, as in [0.4]; after that, autograd does it for you.
hamming.why: A value copied to many places affects the loss through every copy, so by the chain rule its gradient is the sum over all of them.

object.title: The stamp and its prints
object.subtitle: Four pages of corrections that fold down onto the one stamp that made them.

knobs.label: Fold the corrections onto the stamp

cap.1: Four prints of one three-letter stamp. Each print's bars are its red-pen corrections, one per letter.
cap.2: grad_out has shape (4, 3): one gradient row per broadcast copy of b, which is (3,).
cap.3: Upstream gradient ∂L/∂y for y = x + b, with b broadcast along dim 0.

cap.1: Fold the pages onto the stamp: each letter's corrections stack up, and the stamp row now holds the totals.
cap.2: unbroadcast sums over dim 0: b.grad = grad_out.sum(0), shape (3,).
cap.3: Σᵢ ∂L/∂yᵢ per column gives (1.0, 1.2, 1.4) here: the transpose of the copy.

cap.1: Stamp only two pages and the stamp's total is smaller: fewer prints, fewer corrections to add.
cap.2: The summed gradient grows with the number of copies: a value used more often collects more signal.
cap.3: ∂L/∂b has one term per copy; with n = 2 only two rows contribute.

cap.1: Stamp a single page and the fix is exactly that page's correction. No copies, nothing to add.
cap.2: With one copy, unbroadcast only squeezes the prepended dim; the numbers pass through unchanged.
cap.3: n = 1: the sum has a single term, so unbroadcast reduces to removing the size-1 leading axis.

predict.q: A bias of shape (3,) is added to a batch of shape (32, 3). What shape must its gradient be?
predict.why: A gradient always has the shape of the thing it belongs to. Sum the (32, 3) upstream gradient over the batch dim.

predict.q: The stamp was pressed on four pages. How do you combine the four corrections?
predict.why: Nudging the stamp moves all four prints, so all four effects add. Averaging learns four times too slowly; keeping one is the overwrite bug.

predict.q: The original was (4, 1) and got stretched to (4, 3). After summing over dim 1 you should:
predict.why: Stretched size-1 dims are summed with keepdim=True. Only dims prepended at the front are summed away entirely.

object.where: Any shared weight: biases over a batch, conv kernels over positions, embedding rows over tokens.
